opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The key insight is that in a dataflow architecture you're not executing the model one kernel at a time, the way you would on a GPU. On a GPU, each operator is launched separately, reads its inputs from HBM, computes, and writes the results back to HBM, so the next kernel can pick them up. You end up spending a huge amount of your memory bandwidth just moving intermediate results back and forth. And for a lot of modern models, especially in inference, that's what limits you. You're memory-bound, not compute-bound.

So the approach we take is to think of the model as a dataflow graph and map large pieces of that graph spatially onto the chip at once. You take a whole sequence of operators, say an entire decoder layer of a transformer, or even several layers, and lay them out across the compute and on-chip memory units so they run as a pipeline. Data streams from one operator directly into the next through the on-chip interconnect, and the intermediate results stay in on-chip SRAM. We call this operator fusion, but it's much more aggressive than what you can do with kernel fusion on a GPU, because the hardware is designed around it rather than having to hand-write a fused kernel for every combination.

Once you do that, the only traffic that has to go to HBM is what really needs to be there: the weights, the KV cache, and the inputs and outputs of these big fused regions. So the compiler's job becomes figuring out how to partition the graph into those regions, how to allocate on-chip memory and compute among the operators so the pipeline is balanced, and how to schedule HBM accesses so they're large, streaming transfers that keep the bandwidth saturated rather than lots of small random accesses. Balance matters a lot here. If one stage of the pipeline is slower, everything waits on it, so you allocate resources in proportion to each operator's work.

Then there's the broader memory hierarchy. HBM is fast but it's limited in capacity, so we also pair it with a large DDR tier. That lets you hold many models, or very large models, in DDR and bring the active one into HBM quickly. That's what makes things like composition of experts, or serving many fine-tuned models, practical, because you can switch between them in milliseconds instead of being limited by what fits in HBM.

So, in short: fuse aggressively, keep intermediates on-chip, use HBM only for what has to live there, and make sure those accesses are streaming and well scheduled. That's how you get much closer to using all of the bandwidth for useful work, which is where a lot of the inference performance advantage comes from.

r001.rationale: It identifies inference as often memory-bound rather than compute-bound, with HBM bandwidth spent moving intermediate results between operators.

r002.rationale: It explains that mapping operators as a dataflow pipeline streams results directly between them on-chip, keeping intermediates out of HBM.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the first thing to understand is that the whole premise of dataflow is that you're trying to invert the usual relationship between the compute and the memory system. In a GPU, or really any instruction-based architecture, you execute a kernel, you write the result out to HBM, then the next kernel reads it back in. So every operator boundary becomes a round trip through memory, and your performance ends up being bounded by how many bytes you can move, not by how many flops you have. HBM is fast, but it's not fast enough to keep up with the compute if you're doing that for every layer.

So when we map a model onto a dataflow architecture like the SambaNova RDU, the question we're asking is: how much of the model can we keep on chip, flowing from one operator to the next, without ever touching HBM? We take the model's computational graph—the matmuls, the softmax, the layer norm, the activations—and we spatially lay those operators out across the chip, so that the output of one unit streams directly into the input of the next. That's what we call kernel fusion at a very aggressive level, where you're fusing not just a couple of elementwise ops but an entire decoder layer or more into a single dataflow pipeline. The intermediate activations live in on-chip SRAM, and HBM is reserved for the things that actually have to live there, which is primarily the weights and the KV cache.

Once you've done that, the bandwidth problem becomes a scheduling problem. You know exactly what the chip is going to need and when, because the dataflow graph is static, so you can prefetch weights into on-chip memory ahead of when the compute needs them. You're streaming weights in at close to peak HBM bandwidth, continuously, rather than having bursty access patterns where you load a weight tile, compute on it, stall, and go back. And the compiler does most of this—it's doing the partitioning, deciding which operators go where, how to tile the tensors so they fit in the available SRAM, and how to balance the pipeline stages so no stage is starved.

The other piece that matters a lot for inference specifically is that memory capacity and bandwidth interact. With a lot of HBM on the system, you can keep many models or many experts resident, and then the dataflow mapping lets you switch between them without the kind of swapping overhead you'd otherwise see. So for mixture-of-experts models, for example, you're routing tokens to experts whose weights are already in memory and streaming them through fused pipelines, which is where you see the really large gains over a kernel-by-kernel approach.

So the short version is: keep activations on chip, make the weight traffic predictable and continuous, and let the compiler, rather than the programmer, figure out the spatial mapping.

r001.rationale: It identifies repeated transfers through HBM as the performance bottleneck, saying performance is limited by bytes moved rather than compute.

r002.rationale: It explains that operators stream outputs directly to the next operator and keep intermediate activations on chip, avoiding HBM transfers between kernels.

astra-6.text:
The way I think about it is to start with the movement of data. Where are the weights and activations, how often do you need them, and how much computation can you do each time you bring them out of HBM? You want each transfer to support as much useful work as possible.

With a dataflow architecture, you map the operations onto compute resources and arrange for data to flow between them. If one operation produces an intermediate result that the next operation consumes, ideally you keep that on chip rather than write it to HBM and read it back. Then you tile the computation so that the working set fits in local memory, and you reuse those tiles as much as you can.

The other piece is balancing the pipeline. You need enough parallel memory accesses to use the available bandwidth, and you want to overlap those accesses with computation. But if one stage can't consume data at the rate you're supplying it, more bandwidth doesn't help. So the mapping is really a joint problem: allocating compute, allocating on-chip storage, and scheduling communication. The goal is to keep the compute busy while minimizing unnecessary trips to HBM.

r001.rationale: It frames the mapping around data movement to and from HBM, maximizing work per transfer, and using available bandwidth.

r002.rationale: It says to keep an intermediate result on chip for the next operation instead of writing it to HBM and reading it back.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I think about it is that you have to look at the whole computation, not just an individual operator. You have a graph of operations, and you want to map that graph onto the architecture so that data can flow directly from one operation to the next, keeping intermediate results on chip wherever possible.

HBM gives you a lot of bandwidth, but you don’t want to consume it writing an intermediate result out and then reading it back for the next operation. So you look at fusion, you look at how you tile the computation, and you look at where the weights and activations live. The goal is to get as much reuse as you can from every piece of data you bring in.

Then you have to balance the rates across that pipeline. If one stage can’t supply data fast enough, the downstream compute sits idle. So it’s really a joint problem of scheduling computation and managing data movement. You want the HBM transfers to be efficient and overlapped with computation, while the on-chip dataflow does as much of the communication as possible.

r001.rationale: The response discusses using HBM bandwidth efficiently, but does not identify HBM bandwidth as the bottleneck.

r002.rationale: It says data should flow directly between operations, keeping intermediate results on chip to avoid writing them to HBM and reading them back.
